canonical_statement: The study compared empiric clinician-directed heparin dosing with nomogram-based dosing, focusing on the weight-referenced infusion rate associated with therapeutic APTT and the time required to reach therapeutic APTT.
All patients admitted to the cardiology service at the university health science center who received heparin during the study periods were considered for inclusion.

population.label: Cardiology-service patients receiving heparin
inclusion_criteria: Received heparin during the hospital stay

canonical_statement: Phase 1 screened 95 patients and evaluated 88 patients after seven were excluded for missing information; the evaluated cohort included 53 men and 35 women.
Phase 1 evaluated patients had a mean age of 62.5 years and mean total body weight of 81.7 kg.

Phase 1 heparin indications were unstable angina/myocardial infarction in 54 patients, postthrombolytic therapy in 7, heart failure in 10, pulmonary embolism/deep venous thrombosis in 6, and other indications in 11.
Phase 2 screened 156 patients and evaluated 45 patients who received nomogram-guided therapy; the evaluated cohort included 26 men and 19 women.
Phase 2 evaluated patients had a mean age of 61.2 years and mean total body weight of 80.5 kg.

Phase 2 heparin indications were unstable angina/myocardial infarction in 31 patients, postthrombolytic therapy in 3, heart failure in 2, pulmonary embolism/deep venous thrombosis in 1, and other indications in 8.
In phase 1, physicians determined heparin regimens from clinical experience and each patient’s APTT response, and nursing/pharmacy staff made no dosing interventions.

canonical_statement: Routine monitoring specified in the nomogram included daily hematocrit, platelet count every 3 days, guaiac testing of all stools, and visual checks for hematuria.
For this study, therapeutic heparin therapy was defined as a measured APTT between 55 and 95 seconds.

canonical_statement: Bleeding surveillance relied on clinically important “signs of bleeding” documented by caretakers, without a prespecified bleeding definition; investigators also recorded hematocrits.

outcome.definition: No specific study definition; bleeding considered clinically important by caretakers.

canonical_statement: APTT was measured with Automated APTT reagent and a Coag-a-mate X2 photo-optical analyzer that was recalibrated at least three times every 24 hours.
The investigators calculated ideal body weight, body surface area, and blood volume for regression analyses intended to identify a practical patient-specific variable for heparin infusion rate.

Linear regression was used to relate phase 1 therapeutic infusion rate to patient-specific variables; ANOVA compared time to therapeutic APTT, chi-square compared 12- and 24-hour target attainment, and alpha was 0.05.
In phase 1, 66 of 88 evaluated patients (75.0%) achieved a therapeutic APTT at some time during heparin therapy.

canonical_statement: The authors concluded that weight-based nomogram dosing was associated with a higher proportion of cardiology patients reaching the targeted APTT range earlier than empiric dosing.

The authors judged total body weight to be an acceptable and practical dosing variable even though blood volume and body surface area showed somewhat stronger statistical correlations with therapeutic infusion rate.

The authors inferred from the phase 1 bolus analysis that an appropriate initial infusion rate appeared more important than an initial bolus for maintaining therapeutic APTT during the first 24 hours.
Only 45 of 156 phase 2 patients received dosing according to the nomogram and were included, and the authors identified medical-staff cooperation with the nomogram as an implementation difficulty.

The majority of study patients received heparin for acute angina or suspected myocardial infarction, and the authors advised caution in broader application because few venous thromboembolism patients were represented in phase 2.

The study therapeutic APTT range of 55 to 95 seconds could be higher or broader than ranges used elsewhere, and the 95-second upper limit was chosen mainly from investigator clinical experience because a bleeding threshold was not established.
The study did not evaluate how well the nomogram maintained therapeutic APTT after the target range had first been achieved.
Bleeding was not a primary study objective, no specific bleeding definition was used, and minor bleeding not requiring heparin discontinuation may have gone undocumented.

Seven phase 1 patients and three phase 2 patients received recombinant DNA-derived tissue plasminogen activator before heparin, which the authors acknowledged could have influenced APTT and infusion-rate assessment.
The investigators did not compare heparin dosage requirements by indication because some indication groups contained too few patients for useful statistical analysis.
